claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Finding the Northern Arapaho government's own resources
claimBlocks.text: The Northern Arapaho Tribe's website identifies Wind River as its location and links governmental and departmental resources. It offers a starting point for a particular tribal government's public information. Its brief homepage is a navigation source; the linked publications require their own reading and dates before supporting detailed historical or policy claims.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Homepage navigation 0–8, institutional links 14–36 and location statement 39–41

claimBlocks.text: The departmental directory lists an Ethete immersion entry alongside other public services. Such listings help readers find Northern Arapaho institutions. A directory alone does not establish current staffing, availability, teaching methods or results. Detailed claims about educational work need a dated publication that explains its purposes, practices and evidence.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Displayed department listings, especially Immersion (Ethete), lines 88–92; linked brief description reviewed separately

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Education as an expression of self-determination
claimBlocks.text: The Tribe's 2006 Education Code presents education as part of Northern Arapaho self-determination. It prioritizes Arapaho language, history and culture alongside academic learning and parent and community participation. It expressly disclaims authority over Eastern Shoshone education policy. This dated publication documents the Northern Arapaho government's stated priorities; its presence online does not verify implementation, educational outcomes or unchanged current law.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Title 8, section 102 on 2; section 104(c) on 5–6; history/enactment note on 31. Preface i–ii supplies publication and governmental-scope cautions

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Food sovereignty and telling community histories
claimBlocks.text: In a 2019 study, Northern Arapaho researcher Melvin L. Arthur, with Christine M. Porter, relates food sovereignty to community control over historical storytelling. Interviews, talking circles, personal experience and historical research inform his account of disrupted food access and reclamation. He places these changes within colonial dispossession. This is a situated Northern Arapaho interpretation, without demonstrating current clinical outcomes or unanimity among community members.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Printed 70–73 for authorship, purpose, methods and positionality; 80–81 for reclamation discussion and conclusion

inspections.method: Actual Tribe-hosted code index followed to two original PDFs. Normal validated HTTPS downloads succeeded. pypdf confirmed a 31-page Education Code and two-page preface; selected text actually read. No image QA or full-code review claimed.
evidence: Education Code page 2, section 102 expressly says its enactment asserts no authority/jurisdiction over Eastern Shoshone educational goals and policies.
Pages 5–6, section 104(c), combine academic learning, English and Arapaho language competence, tribal history, family/community participation and self-determination as stated policy.
Page 31's history note records enactment by the Northern Arapaho Business Council on May 4, 2006, Resolution 2006-9070; this corroborates the repeated version date rather than relying on a filename.

The complete preface excludes regulations and specified internal-government resolutions from the publication, distinguishes explanatory comments from legislation, and describes separate Northern Arapaho and Eastern Shoshone sovereign authority.
inspections.limits: No claim of unchanged current law, presently enforceable jurisdiction, school compliance, legal eligibility, educational attainment or program effectiveness. Old test/dropout figures and a visible comment's conflicting percentage notation are not used. Underlying federal/state law and treaties are not independently reviewed. Other code titles and current amendments are not read or counted. No seal, flag or media reproduction proposed.

inspections.method: Actual original journal landing and linked full PDF opened. Normal validated HTTPS download succeeded; pypdf confirmed 16 pages. Selected printed 69–73, 80–81 read, including original online-publication date, explicit first-person identity/positionality, methods and conclusion. This is not abstract-only inspection or a claim to review the complete history narrative.
evidence: Printed 70 and 73 explicitly identify Arthur as a Northern Arapaho tribal member and explain his insider perspective; this identity is not inferred from university employment.

Printed 72–73 distinguish the co-author's role and describe Food Dignity and Growing Resilience, interviews in 2013 and 2018, talking circles in 2017–2018, participation/observation, autoethnography and historical research. No claim that these are disjoint representative samples.

Printed 73 reports university, both tribal governments and community-advisory approvals for the relevant research; these are the authors' statements, not new Atlas approvals or an authorization to republish data.

Printed 80–81 discuss food-system reclamation and the author-led historical interpretation. Eastern Shoshone bison and gathering initiatives are explicitly identified as such and are not relabeled Northern Arapaho projects.
inspections.limits: Selected pages only. No creation narratives, ceremonial/prophetic material, participant quotations, sensitive places, health-risk figures, present population, trial outcomes or source figures/media are reproduced. Historical causal interpretation is attributed to the authors, not offered as medical guidance or a tested clinical effect. The first-person 'we' sometimes expands beyond Northern Arapaho; the synthesis preserves its narrower situated scope. Study participation does not establish all-community unanimity. References, related articles and original project datasets were not independently read or counted.

geographyNotes: The actual homepage situates this government's resources at Wind River. The displayed departmental addresses explicitly name Wyoming, including Ethete. These are scoped institutional associations, not a complete historical homeland or boundary map.

The code preface explicitly distinguishes Northern Arapaho and Eastern Shoshone sovereign authority within a shared reservation; Title 8 section 102 reinforces that its education policy does not claim Eastern Shoshone jurisdiction. Shared geography is not a single government or identity.

These sources concern Northern Arapaho institutions and a situated Northern Arapaho author's research. They do not establish Southern Arapaho Oklahoma membership, government, program arrangements or the full Arapaho homeland. No map/canonical edits made.
integrationNotes: Renew p18-s2 and p18-s3 while preserving both exact original URLs. Both remain countsTowardMinimum=false despite actual fresh reading. Preserve the linked Immersion URL as supporting inspection, not another count.

Add ar18-n3 and ar18-n4 as the two substantive units. The Education Code, its preface and index count once as a conservative publication collection. Other titles, individual sections, university/repository copies and references do not add counts.

The generic homepage/directory should not remain sole evidence for detailed current institutional powers, program practices or outcomes. The new code paragraph supplies expressly dated policy evidence; it is not current legal advice.

Keep Northern Arapaho, Eastern Shoshone and Southern Arapaho identity/government distinctions. Arthur's authorial identity is explicit; the paper does not become an official Tribe-wide consensus statement.

Replace overlapping legacy prose rather than append duplicate claims. Recompute full annotation/scope/subscope/body budgets if an overview or retained paragraph cites these sources; only the supplied claim blocks were budgeted here.

Do not automatically assess the whole canonical profile as adequate or complete from this partial packet. Quality and documented limits govern; a twelve-source target is not a quota. No fresh inspection claimed for the other five baseline sources.
researchGaps: A substantial accessible Northern Arapaho government-authored history remains a useful future addition; About and the old history route were not recovered here.

Current education-policy amendments, operational reports and program evaluation would be needed for present-law, service-availability or effectiveness claims. The 2006 code is a dated primary publication.
The 2019 study's selected methods/conclusion offer an authored perspective, not full demographic coverage, clinical findings or direct review of all cited archives and historical narratives.

The current packet contributes only Northern Arapaho-specific renewal and additions; broader Arapaho and Southern Arapaho renewal is assigned separately. No community contact or direct review requested.
